segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: OK, Jack. Before we plan our presentation about refrigeration, let’s discuss what we’ve discovered so far.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Fine, Annie. Though I have to admit I haven’t done much research yet.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: Nor me. But I found an interesting article about icehouses. I’d been some 18th- and 19th-century ones here in the UK, so I knew they were often built in a shady area or underground, close to lakes that might freeze in the winter. Then blocks of ice could be cut and stored in the icehouse. But I didn’t realise that insulating the blocks with straw or sawdust meant they didn’t melt for months [[ ]] . The ancient Romans had refrigeration, too.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: I didn’t know that.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: Yes, pits were dug in the ground, and snow was imported from the mountains – even though they were at quite a distance. The snow was stored in the pits. Ice formed at the bottom of it. Both the ice and the snow were then sold [[ ]] . The ice cost more than the snow and my guess is that only the wealthy members of society could afford it.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: I wouldn’t be surprised. I also came across an article about modern domestic fridges. Several different technologies are used, but they were too complex for me to understand.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: You have to wonder what happens when people get rid of old ones.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: You mean because the gases in them are harmful for the environment?

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: Exactly. At least these are now plenty of organisations that will recycle most of the components safety, but of course some people just dump old fridges in the countryside. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: It’s hard to see how they can be stopped unfortunately [[ ]] . In the UK we get rid of three million a year altogether!

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: That sounds a lot, especially because fridges hardly ever break down.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: That’s right. In this country we keep domestic fridges for 11 years on average, and a lot last for 20 or more. So if you divide the cost by the number of years you can use a fridge, they’re not expensive, compared with some household appliances. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: True. I suppose manufactures encourage people to spend more by making them different colours and designs. I’m sure when my parents bought their first fridge they had hardly any choice!

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Yes, there’s been quite a change. ———————–

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Right, let’s make a list of topics to cover in our presentation, and decide who’s going to do more research on them. Then later, we can get together and plan the next step.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: OK. How about starting with how useful refrigeration is, and the range of goods that are refrigerated [[ ]] nowadays? Because of course it’s not just food and drinks.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: No, I suppose flowers and medicines are refrigerated, too.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: And computers. I could do that [[ ]] , unless you particularly want to.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: No, that’s fine by me. What about the effects of refrigeration on people’s health [[ ]] ? After all, some of the chemicals used in the 19th century were pretty harmful, but there have been lots of benefits too, like always have access to fresh food. Do you fancy dealing with that?

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: I’m no terribly keen, to be honest.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Nor me. My mind just goes blank when I read anything about chemicals.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: Oh, all right then, I’ll do you a favour [[ ]] . But you own me, Jack. What about the effects on food producers, like farmers in poorer countries being able to export their produce to developed countries? Something for you, maybe?

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: I don’t mind. It should be quite interesting.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: I think we should also look at how refrigeration has helped whole cities [[ ]] – like Las Vegas, which couldn’t exist without refrigeration because it’s in the middle of a desert.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Right. I had a quick look at an economics book in the library that’s got a chapter about this sort of thing. I could give you the title, if you want to do this section.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: Not particularly, to be honest. I find economics books pretty heavy going, as a rule.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: OK, leave it to me, then.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: Thanks. Then there’s transport, and the difference that refrigerated trucks [[ ]] have made. I wouldn’t mind having a go at that.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Don’t forget trains, too. I read something about milk and butter being transported in refrigerated railroad cars in the USA, right back in the 1840s.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: I hadn’t thought of trains. Thanks.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: Shall we have a separate section on domestic fridges [[ ]] ? After all, they’re something everyone’s familiar with.

segments.speaker: ANNIE
segments.en: What about splitting it into two? You could investigate 19th- and 20th-century fridges, and I’ll concentrate on what’s available these days, and how manufacturers differentiate their products from those of their competitors.

segments.speaker: JACK
segments.en: OK, that’d suit me.
